claims.text: Replacing TOR-TILD's conventional EAM reference with a DNN potential will significantly improve reference–target phase-space overlap in high-temperature multicomponent HEAs.
The proposed method applies to both solid and liquid states near the melting temperature.
The relevant temperature range is approximately 0.8–1.0 Tm.
Equimolar Ti-Zr-Ta-Hf-Nb is an example of the refractory HEA composition to which the intervention applies.
The replacement DNN potential should be trained on ab initio data spanning a wide range of liquid atomic configurations.
A DNN potential has been used to describe both solid and liquid states of a Ti-Zr-Ta-Hf-Nb-based high-entropy material and to predict its melting behavior.
The intervention is applicable to equimolar or near-equimolar refractory HEAs and other multicomponent systems near or above 0.8 Tm.
Learning from broad ab initio liquid configurations enables the DNN to capture local atomic environments in a disordered liquid.
Capturing those local liquid environments makes the DNN reference thermodynamic phase space more closely match the ab initio target phase space.
EAM references have fixed functional forms and limited representations of configurations.
DNN potentials can adapt to the complex many-body interactions present in an ab initio liquid better than EAM references.
Improved representation of liquid configurations reduces mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
The DNN reference will produce a measurable and significant reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
Under equivalent integration conditions, the free-energy error could decrease by a factor of two or more.
Current EAM-based TOR-TILD implementations exhibit noticeable path mismatch because they cannot capture the configuration diversity of HEA liquids.
The intervention should be most effective in stable high-entropy liquids with extensive configurational disorder and may not transfer to less-disordered systems or temperatures far below Tm.
The amount of improvement depends on the quality and representativeness of the DNN training data, the degree of liquid disorder, and transferability across alloy systems.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant path-mismatch reduction, or failure to improve melting-temperature accuracy against an independent benchmark, would falsify the hypothesis.
